claims.text: The studied alloy has composition Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Rapid cooling can retain Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a metastable high-temperature BCC structure.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a balance between the BCC–FCC Gibbs free-energy difference and kinetic barriers to transformation.
The Gibbs free-energy difference in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 thermodynamically favors FCC over BCC in the proposed annealing regime.
Differences in Gibbs free energy between BCC and FCC phases can correlate with phase stability and transformation rate in multicomponent alloys.
Sluggish diffusion is reported in high-entropy alloys and can kinetically affect phase selection.
Sluggish atomic diffusion specifically delays FCC nucleation and growth in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Annealing at approximately 700–900 °C provides appreciable diffusion in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 without causing extraneous degradation.
Thermally activated local atomic diffusion and interfacial rearrangement enable a BCC-to-FCC transformation.
Increasing thermal exposure should increase the FCC phase fraction and decrease the residual BCC fraction in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Minimal thermal exposure should preserve the metastable BCC state.
Sufficient annealing should drive the metastable BCC alloy toward an equilibrium, FCC-dominated microstructure.
The transformation requires a temperature and dwell-time regime sufficient to activate diffusion.
Excessive annealing temperature may produce undesired phases in this alloy.
XRD, EBSD, and TEM can be used to quantify or confirm changes in BCC and FCC phase fractions and transformation morphology.
A statistically significant failure of extended annealing to increase the FCC fraction relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
The exact BCC–FCC free-energy difference and diffusion parameters for this alloy are not precisely known.
Slight compositional inhomogeneities may influence the thermodynamic–kinetic interplay.
